input.question: Why is it that when I'm really drunk I can barely taste what I'm drinking, but I feel like I'm hypersensitive to how food tastes?
input.ground_truth: Because you are becoming taste blind to the beer over time. If you sit in a room that has a nice smell you'll eventually not be able to smell it over time. Same thing applies if you drink Keystone all night (the fact that it has a mild taste and makes you intoxicated only amplifies the effect) but if you eat something that is very flavorful then it makes a greater impression.

Question: Why is it that when I'm really drunk I can barely taste what I'm drinking, but I feel like I'm hypersensitive to how food tastes?

response.prediction:
Okay, let's imagine you have a big toy box full of different toys (these are like your taste buds in your mouth). When you’re not drunk, all your toys are working and playing together, so you can feel and taste everything—sweet, sour, salty, and so on.

But when you drink a lot of alcohol (get really drunk), it’s like someone puts a blanket over most of your toys. So now, you can’t really feel or taste your drink very well—that’s why the drink doesn’t taste very strong to you.

However, your mouth and tongue are still kind of awake, and sometimes, when you eat food, it’s like giving your toys a big, fun job to do all at once. That’s why food can taste super strong or even more exciting than usual. It’s like your toys are waking up a little to play with the food, even if they’re still a bit sleepy from the alcohol.

So, when you’re really drunk, drinks taste less, but food tastes a lot!
